hints: Look at where X is placed in the circuit, in series with the power supply and electrodes, and think which electrical quantity must be measured to use $Q = It$ later.
walkthrough:
Read the circuit as an electrolysis circuit**
You have a power supply driving current through two silver electrodes, with a variable resistor to keep the current steady. To find the total charge passed you will need both current and time, so current must be measured continuously during the 40.0 minutes.
Final answer: X is an ammeter.

hints: Think about which ion must be present in solution so that silver metal can deposit cleanly at the cathode by $\text{Ag}^{+} + \text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Ag}$ without other ions competing.
walkthrough:
Link the electrodes to the ions needed**
Both electrodes are silver. At the cathode silver ions are discharged: $\text{Ag}^{+} + \text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Ag}$. At the anode silver dissolves: $\text{Ag} \rightarrow \text{Ag}^{+} + \text{e}^{-}$. So the solution must supply $\text{Ag}^{+}$ ions from the start.

Choose a soluble silver salt with an inert anion**
A solution of silver nitrate, $\text{AgNO}_{3}$, is ideal because it is soluble and the nitrate ion is not discharged in preference to silver. $\text{AgF}$ or $\text{AgClO}_{4}$ work in the same way.

hints: Start from the cathode mass gain, use $n = m/M_{r}$ with $M_{r}(\text{Ag}) = 107.9$ to get moles of $\text{Ag}$ deposited.
Convert the electrolysis time to seconds and use $Q = It$ to get total coulombs, then divide by the charge on one electron to count the electrons.
Remember one $\text{Ag}^{+}$ needs one electron, so dividing total electrons passed by moles of $\text{Ag}$ formed gives electrons per mole, which is $L$.
walkthrough:
Find moles of silver deposited**
Mass gained is pure silver metal. Use:
$$n(\text{Ag}) = \frac{m}{M_{r}}$$
$$n(\text{Ag}) = \frac{0.500}{107.9} = 4.63 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$
This tells you how many moles of $\text{Ag}^{+}$ ions were discharged.

Find total charge and total electrons**
Charge is current multiplied by time in seconds:
$$Q = It$$
$$Q = 0.200 \times 40.0 \times 60 = 480 \text{ C}$$
Each electron carries $1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, so:
$$\text{number of electrons} = \frac{Q}{e} = \frac{480}{1.60 \times 10^{-19}} = 3.00 \times 10^{21}$$
Be careful to convert minutes to seconds, a very common slip.

Scale up to one mole to get L**
The cathode equation is $\text{Ag}^{+} + \text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Ag}$, so moles of electrons equals moles of silver. Divide the number of particles by the number of moles:
$$L = \frac{\text{number of electrons}}{n(\text{Ag})}$$
$$L = \frac{3.00 \times 10^{21}}{4.634 \times 10^{-3}} = 6.47 \times 10^{23} \text{ mol}^{-1}$$
That is the number of electrons needed to deposit $1 \text{ mol}$ of silver, which is the Avogadro constant.

Final answer: moles $\text{Ag} = 0.500/107.9 = 4.63 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$
$Q = 0.200 \times 40.0 \times 60 = 480 \text{ C}$
number of electrons $= 480 / 1.60 \times 10^{-19} = 3.00 \times 10^{21}$
electrons per mole $= 3.00 \times 10^{21} / 4.63 \times 10^{-3} = 6.47 \times 10^{23}$
